from pypdf import PdfReader

reader=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')

    text.append(f'\\n\\n======== PAGE {i+1} ========\\n\\n'+t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(text))
print(''.join(text)[:26000])

folder=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for path in folder.glob('page-*.png'):
    path.unlink()
(folder/'manuscript.txt').unlink()
folder.rmdir()
Path('tmp').rmdir()
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem in sparse-reward MARL. Its observation that increasing the number of agents can make tasks easier motivates adaptive curricula beyond conventional few-to-more schedules.

SPMARL offers a simple integration of self-paced curriculum optimization with MAPPO, reusing critic loss to score tasks. Parameter sharing and observation padding provide practical mechanisms for transferring policies across agent counts.

Experiments cover three structurally different settings and demonstrate substantial benefits from adaptive curricula over direct target-task training. SPMARL shows promising early learning gains over SPRL in Simple-Spread and SMACv2. Curriculum trajectories aid interpretation, and the paper supplies five-seed confidence intervals for Simple-Spread and a code link.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of critic loss as learning progress is insufficiently justified. Equation 8 measures prediction error: even under a fixed policy with an exact value function, squared return error can remain positive because of conditional return variance. Large loss can therefore reflect stochasticity or poor critic fitting without indicating useful policy improvement. No direct measurements establish the claimed relationship to policy change or reduced credit-assignment difficulty. This leaves the main mechanism unsupported despite the promising heuristic.

The comparisons do not establish superiority over relevant curriculum alternatives. A linear schedule cannot represent the full contributions of methods such as VACL and EPC. In Simple-Spread, the only linear baseline increases agent count, although the paper explicitly explains why this direction is unfavorable; a tuned decreasing or performance-triggered schedule is an essential comparison. Learning-progress-based curriculum baselines are also missing.

The novelty discussion omits closely related value-error-based task prioritization, particularly Prioritized Level Replay (Jiang et al., ICML 2021). This omission matters because the proposed novelty centers on using critic loss instead of reward to select tasks. The MARL adaptation could still constitute a useful contribution, but its relationship to existing approaches needs clearer positioning and empirical comparison.

Evidence for consistently faster convergence than SPRL is limited. The XOR evaluation curves nearly coincide, and final performance is generally comparable. Quantified learning-speed measures with uncertainty would better support the principal empirical claim. Seed counts are stated only for Simple-Spread, and there are no sensitivity studies for the performance threshold or initial context distribution, although these directly control curriculum behavior.

The teacher optimization is not mathematically executable as specified. Equation 6 minimizes KL(p || mu) while describing mu as a Dirac delta; this divergence is infinite for a nondegenerate Gaussian curriculum. The actual target approximation and treatment of discretization/clipping need specification. Algorithm 1 also returns to Stage 1 whenever performance falls below the threshold, whereas Section 4.1 describes freezing the context distribution after entering Stage 2.

Reproduction requires substantial missing information, including complete context initialization and bounds, KL budgets, teacher update frequency, per-task thresholds, network architectures, and training settings. The XOR experiment particularly needs to explain how shared policies distinguish agents and accommodate action spaces that change with agent count. These details affect both solvability and transfer, so deferring implementation information to code is insufficient for assessing the reported results.

Minor presentation inconsistencies should be corrected: Section 5.3 refers to an eight-agent target despite evaluating five versus five, and several passages call the Random curriculum a random policy even though its student is trained. These issues are secondary to the methodological and evidential concerns above.
